title: We Drained the Water Under the Mackinac Bridge. Here's What Was Hidden.

sections.title: Five miles of water
sections.dir: Quiet and gripping, like the start of a true mystery. Pause after each item in the first paragraph. "So let's drain it." is said plainly, with a small pause before it. The last paragraph is warmer and direct.
paras: Under the Mackinaw Bridge, there's a shipwreck that took ten men. Two oil pipelines carrying millions of gallons a day. A bridge worker who never came home. And a waterfall that no one saw for thousands of years.
All of it hidden in water up to two hundred and ninety-five feet deep. Millions of people have driven across this bridge. Almost none of them know what's underneath it.
So let's drain it.
We can't really, of course. But lake-bed maps, sonar and divers have shown us what's down there. So we're going to lower the water, a few feet at a time, and watch what appears.
And at the very bottom is something that, if it ever broke, could spread oil along hundreds of miles of shoreline.

This is Great Lakes Files. We go looking for the places hidden in and under these lakes. Most of the people watching these videos haven't subscribed yet, so if you like this kind of story, tap subscribe right now. It's free, it takes one second, and it's what keeps this channel going.

sections.title: The drain begins
sections.dir: Brisk and vivid, like a countdown. A short pause after each depth ("Ten feet." "Twenty feet."). The last line drops lower, with suspense.
paras: Let's start the drain.
Ten feet. Off Mackinaw Island, a jumble of ancient broken rock starts to break the surface. Divers call it the Rock Maze.
Twenty feet. The shoreline creeps outward on both sides. The islands grow. The five-mile gap between Michigan's two peninsulas starts to narrow.
Thirty feet. Between the bridge towers, the water is still deep and dark. But a few miles to the east, just under the surface, something long is waiting.

sections.title: Thirty-five feet
sections.dir: Storytelling, building tension. Quote the lookout plainly. A real pause after "Neither did." and after "Ten of the thirty-five men died."
paras: At thirty-five feet, a few miles east of the bridge, something long and dark breaks the surface. The top of a ship's hull.

Her name is the Cedarville. Five hundred and eighty-eight feet long. On the morning of May the seventh, nineteen sixty-five, she was carrying more than fourteen thousand tons of limestone through the Straits, with thirty-five men on board.
The fog that morning was so thick that two ships had already run aground near the Soo, and another had crashed into a lighthouse. The Cedarville kept going at full speed.
On the radar, her officers could see ships ahead. A Norwegian freighter, the Topdalsfjord, was coming the other way. Each captain thought the other knew what he was going to do. Neither did.
The lookout shouted, "There she is!" The Norwegian ship's bow, built strong for breaking ice, came out of the fog and tore a hole in the Cedarville, below the waterline.
The crew tried to cover the hole with a tarp. It was too big. The captain turned toward a beach about four miles away, to run her aground before she could sink.
She didn't make it. At ten twenty-five that morning, still two miles short of the beach, the Cedarville rolled onto her side and went down.
Ten of the thirty-five men died.
With the water gone, you'd see her lying on the bottom in two pieces, a hundred and ten feet down. Since then, three divers have lost their lives exploring her.

sections.title: Sixty-five feet
sections.dir: Calm, with a quiet sense of warning. Slow down for the last paragraph.
paras: At sixty-five feet, just west of the bridge, two dark lines come up out of the lake bed and run across the bottom, side by side, toward the other shore.
They're oil pipelines. Together they're called Line Five. They were laid across the Straits in nineteen fifty-three, four years before the bridge was finished.

Each pipe is twenty inches wide. They run four and a half miles across the lake bed, from one peninsula to the other. Every day, they carry nearly twenty-three million gallons of crude oil and natural gas liquids from western Canada.
Close to shore, the pipes are buried. But out here, past sixty-five feet, they simply lie on the bottom, in the open, held up on supports.
Remember them. Because the deeper we go, the more there is to say about these two pipes.

sections.title: The waterfall
sections.dir: Wonder, slower. Let the waterfall be a real surprise. End on a question.
paras: As the water keeps falling, off the east side of Mackinaw Island, something appears that makes no sense in the middle of a lake.
A cliff. A wall of rock about a hundred feet high.
It's a waterfall. It was discovered in August, two thousand seven, and named Mackinaw Falls.
Except no water has poured over it for thousands of years. It sits at the bottom of a lake.
So how does a waterfall end up a hundred feet underwater? Hold on to that question. The answer is at the very bottom.

sections.title: The graveyard
sections.dir: Low and steady, like walking through a cemetery. Read the ship names slowly, with a short pause after each. The last paragraph is direct and friendly.
paras: As the water keeps falling, the Straits start to look like a graveyard.
Thick fog and crowded shipping lanes have sunk ship after ship here. Half a dozen lighthouses stand around it for a reason.
Today, this water is a protected shipwreck preserve, a hundred and forty-eight square miles of it, with at least twenty-two wrecks that divers can visit, and more lying deeper.

The Sandusky, at around eighty feet. The M. Stalker, at eighty-five. The William Young, at a hundred and twenty. The Minneapolis, at a hundred and twenty-four. The Eber Ward, between a hundred and eleven and a hundred and forty-five.
Now the whole of the Cedarville is out of the water too, lying in her two halves.

Before we go any deeper, take a guess. What's the strangest thing at the very bottom of the Straits? A ship? The pipelines? Or something far older? Put your guess in the comments right now. One word is enough. Then see if you were right.
And stay with me. The deepest part of the Straits still holds the answer to that waterfall, and the rest of the story of those two pipes.

sections.title: Two hundred and ten feet
sections.dir: Respectful and serious. Read each worker's story simply, without drama. A real pause after "Koppen's body was never recovered."
paras: As the water falls toward two hundred feet, the bridge itself starts to look different. It opened on November the first, nineteen fifty-seven. It's five miles long, and its two towers rise five hundred and fifty-two feet above the water. But they don't stop at the waterline. Their foundations go down another two hundred and ten feet. Each tower stands more than seven hundred and sixty feet from its base to its top. Drivers only ever see part of it.
Building them took four summers, with no work in the winter, at a cost of a hundred million dollars. And five men.
In September, nineteen fifty-four, a diver named Frank Pepper came up too fast from a hundred and forty feet down. He died of the bends.
A month later, James LeSarge lost his balance and fell forty feet into one of the foundations. Two weeks after that, Albert Abbott fell from a narrow beam into the water.

On June the sixth, nineteen fifty-six, a catwalk near the north tower collapsed. Jack Baker and Robert Koppen, both twenty-eight, fell. It was their first day on the job. Koppen's body was never recovered.
People like to say there are workers buried inside the bridge. There aren't. But one of them was never found.

And the bridge has taken lives since. In September, nineteen seventy-eight, a small plane flying through heavy fog hit one of the bridge's cables. The wings tore off, and the plane fell into the Straits. All three men on board were killed.

sections.title: Two hundred and seventy feet
sections.dir: Measured and fair, like a careful reporter. Slow down for "aren't really two lakes" and for the shoreline numbers. Give Enbridge's side the same calm weight.
paras: Under the middle of the bridge, the water was two hundred and fifty feet deep. Now it's gone. And here, at about two hundred and seventy feet, the two pipelines reach their lowest point, lying across the floor of the Straits.

Remember I said there was more to say about them. They're more than seventy years old. In two thousand fourteen, Enbridge, the company that runs them, was found not to be keeping the pipe supports as close together as required. And the company says that, although the pipes are in good condition, their outer coating has worn away in places.
Then, in two thousand eighteen, a tugboat's anchor hit the pipeline and dented it.
The dent was less than an inch deep. The pipe held.

But it showed what could happen. And here's why that matters so much. Lake Michigan and Lake Huron aren't really two lakes. The water through the Straits keeps them at the same level, so scientists count them as one, the largest freshwater lake on Earth by area. And that water surges through here, sometimes east, sometimes west, at times more than two and a half million cubic feet every second.
A study by the University of Michigan found that a leak here could reach about seven hundred miles of shoreline, and up to sixty percent of Lake Huron's open water.

Enbridge says the pipes under the Straits have never leaked, and that they're watched around the clock and inspected by underwater robots. Michigan sued in two thousand nineteen to shut this section down. Canada has stepped in to defend the pipeline. And a tunnel to carry it through the rock beneath the Straits has been planned since two thousand eighteen.
For now, the two pipes are still here, lying on the bottom.

sections.title: The river
sections.dir: Wonder, slow and vivid, like describing a lost world. Then warm and sincere for the last paragraph.
paras: Now, the very bottom. Two hundred and ninety-five feet down, the deepest point of the Straits. And with the water gone, you can finally see what this place really is.
It's a canyon.

About nine thousand years ago, as the last ice age ended, the lakes here were hundreds of feet lower than today. Where Lake Michigan is now, there was a smaller lake that geologists call Lake Chippewa. And its water poured out through a narrow canyon, right here, where the bridge stands today.
There was a river under the Mackinaw Bridge. And on its way east, it went over a waterfall.
Mackinaw Falls.
Then the water rose, and rose, until the canyon, the river and the waterfall all disappeared beneath the lake.

In Lake Huron, archaeologists have found at least sixty stone structures on a ridge that is now deep underwater. They appear to be hunting blinds, built about nine thousand years ago by people hunting caribou on what was then dry land. The world under these lakes wasn't empty. People lived there.

If that just changed the way you see the Mackinaw Bridge, do two things for me right now. Tap the like button, and if you haven't yet, subscribe. For a small channel like this one, that's the difference between this story reaching a few hundred people or a few hundred thousand.

sections.title: Let the water back
sections.dir: Gentle and reflective, slower. Pause between the things disappearing. The last paragraph is direct and friendly.
paras: Now let the water back in.

The river canyon fills first. Then the waterfall disappears. Then the pipelines. The water climbs the bridge towers until only the part we know is left above it. The Cedarville slips under, then the top of her hull, thirty-five feet down. Then the Rock Maze, and the lake is calm again.
Tomorrow, thousands of cars will cross this bridge. Freighters will pass under it. And almost nobody will think about what's lying in the dark below them.

If you live near the Straits, or you've crossed the bridge, dived these wrecks, or worked on the boats here, I'd really like to hear from you. What do you know about what's down there? Tell me in the comments. Some of the best parts of these stories come from people like you, and the best ones might end up in a future video.

sections.title: Your call
sections.dir: Fair and calm for the question. Then warm and direct for the last paragraph, like saying goodnight to a friend.
paras: So here's my question for you. Two oil pipelines, more than seventy years old, lying on the bottom of the largest freshwater lake on Earth by area. Should they stay where they are? Move into a tunnel under the rock? Or be shut down? Tell me what you think in the comments. I read every one.

And if you've watched all the way to here, you're exactly who this channel is made for. So if you haven't subscribed yet, do it now, and tap the bell. Because next, we're going to drain the Graveyard of the Great Lakes, the stretch of Lake Superior where the Edmund Fitzgerald went down. I'd like you to be there when we do. Thanks for watching.
